proof_summary: For a composite with a proper odd prime divisor \(p\), Fermat’s theorem gives the product enough \(p\)-adic valuation beyond that of \((n-1)!\), forcing \(p\mid a(n-1)\) and hence impossibly \(p\mid 2^{n-2}\); the remaining case \(n=2^r\) is excluded by Legendre’s binary digit-sum formula, which gives \(v_2(a(2^r-1))=r-1<r\). Once \(n\) is prime, if the order \(d\) of 2 were less than \(n-1\), then \(n\mid 2^d-1\) would make \(n\) divide the defining product, while the assumed divisibility and the factorial–product identity would then force \(n\mid(n-1)!\), a contradiction.
